title: $1 AI Guardrails: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Finetuned ModernBERTs – Diego Carpintero
talk_summary: Diego Carpintero surveys LLM attack vectors (prompt injection, indirect/RAG poisoning, MCP tool-description asymmetry, agentic RCE) and argues LLMs have no native separation of trusted instructions from untrusted data. He then fine-tunes a ModernBERT encoder as a cheap, self-hosted, ~35ms safe/unsafe classifier guardrail, reaching ~85% accuracy on unseen benchmarks.

takeaways.technique: Cheap self-hosted encoder classifier as a guardrail checkpoint
takeaways.what_they_do: Fine-tune a ModernBERT encoder with a classification head on labeled safe/unsafe data (Inject Guard, 75k examples) and run it as a fast binary discriminator at input/output checkpoints instead of an LLM judge.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the results that we're getting is almost 85% accuracy using only 35 milliseconds per classification
takeaways.numbers: ~85% accuracy, 35-40ms per classification, base model ~150M params, large adds ~6 points accuracy

takeaways.technique: Treat tool descriptions and fetched content as untrusted data
takeaways.what_they_do: Highlights the MCP asymmetry where users approve a one-line tool summary but the model reads the full description containing hidden instructions; recommends safety checks on MCP tool descriptions, RAG chunks, and agentic plans, not just user prompts.
takeaways.evidence_quote: what the LLM reads is the full description. And this can contain hidden instructions

takeaways.technique: Encoder discriminator as a cheap first-pass reviewer gate
takeaways.what_they_do: Argues classification tasks (is this safe/unsafe, does this match a policy) are better served by fine-tuned encoders than generative LLM judges because of latency and cost, and encoders can be retrained in hours as attacks evolve.
takeaways.evidence_quote: an encoder model can be retrained cheaply within within a matter of hours
takeaways.numbers: retrain in hours; 70% memory savings with flash attention + alternating attention

takeaways.technique: Self-host small models to avoid per-token external cost and privacy leakage
takeaways.what_they_do: Self-hosting the fine-tuned encoder avoids sending internal requests, intermediate steps, and model responses to external providers, which compounds token cost and privacy risk.
takeaways.evidence_quote: this will about avoid sending all our internal requests intermediate intermediate steps model responses to external providers
takeaways.numbers: under $1 to build the defensive layer

takeaways.technique: Flash attention + bf16 + memory-efficient optimizer for cheap fine-tuning
takeaways.what_they_do: Uses flash attention, Google bf16, and a memory-efficient Adam optimizer to cut fine-tuning memory ~70% and enable batch size 64, making fine-tuning feasible on commodity hardware.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we managed to reach around 70% memory savings
takeaways.numbers: ~70% memory savings; bf16 cut training memory ~40%; batch size 64
